title: Lithium tried for mania in Melbourne
summary: In 1949 the psychiatrist John Cade reported that lithium salts calmed patients with mania at a veterans' hospital in Melbourne, reviving a forgotten substance as a psychiatric treatment.
explanation:
John Cade was working at the Bundoora Repatriation Hospital, a veterans' hospital on the edge of Melbourne, when he began experiments based on a theory that mania might be caused by a toxic substance in the body. Giving lithium salts to laboratory animals, he noticed that they became calmer.

He then gave lithium citrate and lithium carbonate to ten patients with mania. Several improved strikingly, and he published the results in the Medical Journal of Australia in 1949. Lithium had been used in medicine in the nineteenth century, but its psychiatric use had been forgotten.

Cade's report was an uncontrolled case series. In Denmark, Mogens Schou tested lithium for mania in a trial that allocated patients to lithium or placebo, published in 1954. Uptake was uneven: the United States approved lithium only in 1970, becoming the 50th country to do so.

date.basis: Year of publication of Cade's report.

people.name: Mogens Schou
people.role: Ran a placebo-controlled trial in Denmark (published 1954)

whatChanged: Introduced the first drug shown to have a specific effect on a major mental illness in the modern era.
whyItMattered: Lithium remains a standard treatment for bipolar disorder, and Cade's report helped open the era of psychiatric drug treatment.
limitations: Cade's ten patients were not compared with a control group; firmer evidence came from later controlled trials.
His original theory about a toxin causing mania was not borne out.

sources.citation: Cade JFJ. Lithium salts in the treatment of psychotic excitement (Medical Journal of Australia, 1949). Reprinted in Bulletin of the World Health Organization 2000;78(4):518–520.

title: Artemisinin extracted from qinghao
summary: Working within China's secret national malaria programme, Project 523, Tu Youyou's group found that a low-temperature extract of qinghao (Artemisia annua) cleared malaria parasites in animals in 1971 and in patients in 1972.
explanation:
In the 1960s Chinese military institutes began confidential research on drugs against malaria, and in 1967 a national office was set up to coordinate the work, known as Project 523. In 1969 Tu Youyou, at the Institute of Chinese Materia Medica in Beijing, was appointed to lead a group searching traditional Chinese medicine for candidates.

Early extracts of qinghao gave inconsistent results. A passage in Ge Hong's Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies describes soaking the herb in cold water and wringing out the juice, rather than boiling it. Suspecting that heat destroyed the active ingredient, Tu's group changed to low-temperature extraction. On 4 October 1971, sample 191, an ether extract, completely inhibited malaria parasites in rodents.

Between August and October 1972 the extract was tested on 21 patients in Hainan, all of whom lost their fever and parasites, and on further patients in Beijing. Other institutions helped determine the structure of the active compound, artemisinin. Artemisinin-based combination therapies later became the standard treatment for falciparum malaria worldwide.

date.basis: Successful animal test on 4 October 1971; first clinical tests August–October 1972.

people.name: Tu Youyou and her research group

people.role: Collaborating institutes, including those that determined the chemical structure

people.name: Ge Hong
people.role: Author of the early handbook whose recipe suggested cold extraction

whatChanged: Produced a new class of fast-acting antimalarial drug at a time when parasites were becoming resistant to older drugs.
whyItMattered: Artemisinin derivatives are the core of first-line malaria treatment worldwide.
limitations: Artemisinin emerged from a large, state-directed collaborative programme; many scientists and institutions contributed beyond the group Tu led.
Parasite resistance to artemisinin has since emerged and spread, so it is not a permanent solution.

title: Stomach ulcers traced to a bacterium
summary: In Perth, the pathologist Robin Warren and the physician Barry Marshall showed that curved bacteria, later named Helicobacter pylori, live in the stomach and cause gastritis and most peptic ulcers.
explanation:
Robin Warren noticed small curved bacteria on stomach biopsies, in the lower part of the stomach of about half of patients examined, always alongside inflammation. Together with Barry Marshall, he set out to test the link. After several failed attempts, Marshall succeeded in growing the bacterium in culture in 1982.

At the time, stress and lifestyle were considered the main causes of peptic ulcer, and the idea that bacteria could survive in the acid stomach met resistance. Marshall and Warren went on to show that the bacterium causes gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.

Peptic ulcer disease, often chronic and recurrent, became curable with a short course of antibiotics and acid-reducing drugs.

date.basis: Year in which the bacterium was cultured and the discovery made, as dated by the Nobel Assembly.

people.name: J. Robin Warren
people.role: Pathologist; first linked the bacteria to inflammation

people.name: Barry J. Marshall
people.role: Physician; cultured the bacterium and showed its role in ulcers

whatChanged: Reclassified most peptic ulcers as an infectious disease that antibiotics can cure.
whyItMattered: Turned a chronic, recurring condition into a curable one, and showed how an established consensus can be overturned by evidence.
limitations: Not all ulcers are caused by H. pylori; anti-inflammatory drugs are another major cause.
Most people infected with H. pylori never develop an ulcer.

sources.citation: The Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet. Press release: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2005. 3 October 2005.
sources.supports: Warren, a pathologist from Perth, saw curved bacteria in about 50% of biopsies; discovery dated 1982; Marshall cultivated the bacterium; stress and lifestyle previously considered the major causes; cure with antibiotics and acid secretion inhibitors.

title: The virus that causes AIDS is isolated
summary: In 1983 Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, Luc Montagnier and colleagues at the Institut Pasteur isolated a new retrovirus from the lymph node of a patient at risk of AIDS. It became known as HIV.
explanation:
By the early 1980s many researchers suspected that AIDS had an infectious cause, and the Paris team decided to test whether it might be a retrovirus. The Paris team cultured lymph node cells from patients with swollen lymph glands and early signs of immune damage, and detected a new retrovirus, which they called lymphadenopathy-associated virus (LAV), publishing in Science in 1983.

In 1984, Robert Gallo's group at the US National Institutes of Health reported a virus from many patients, named HTLV-III, and Jay Levy's group in San Francisco separately identified a related virus. The viruses proved to be the same, and in 1985 an international committee named it human immunodeficiency virus.

Identifying the virus led to blood tests that protected blood supplies and allowed diagnosis, and to antiretroviral drugs. Combination therapy greatly extended life expectancy where it was available; the drugs suppress the virus but do not cure the infection.

Treatment controls HIV but does not cure it.

title: Modified mRNA, from a 2005 finding to COVID-19 vaccines
summary: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman found in 2005 that chemically modified building blocks stop synthetic mRNA from triggering inflammation. Their work enabled the mRNA vaccines against COVID-19 approved in December 2020.
explanation:
Using messenger RNA to make the body produce a vaccine antigen had been proposed decades earlier, but synthetic mRNA provoked inflammation and produced little protein. Working at the University of Pennsylvania, Karikó and Weissman showed that immune cells treat unmodified synthetic mRNA as foreign, and that changing its nucleoside bases almost abolished the reaction. They published in 2005; later studies showed that modified mRNA also produces much more protein.

When the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic began, this groundwork, combined with other advances and very large public and private investment, allowed two base-modified mRNA vaccines to be developed and tested at unprecedented speed. Both were approved in December 2020, with reported protection of around 95% against disease in their trials.

date.basis: Key publication in 2005; vaccine approvals in December 2020.

whatChanged: Made mRNA usable as a vaccine platform by removing its inflammatory effect and increasing protein production.
whyItMattered: Enabled highly effective COVID-19 vaccines within a year of the pandemic's start, and a platform now applied to other diseases.
limitations: The 2020 vaccines also depended on other advances, including lipid delivery and stabilised spike proteins.
Global access to COVID-19 vaccines was very unequal, especially in 2021.

sources.citation: The Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet. Press release: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2023.
sources.supports: University of Pennsylvania; 2005 publication on base modifications abolishing inflammatory responses; 2008 and 2010 studies on protein production; two vaccines approved in December 2020 with ~95% reported protection.

sources.supports: Concept proposed over 30 years earlier; stabilised spike antigen and large investments also required; approval of two vaccines in late 2020.

title: Smallpox eradicated
summary: After an intensified WHO-led campaign launched in 1967, the last natural case of smallpox occurred in Merca, Somalia, in October 1977. In May 1980 the World Health Assembly declared the disease eradicated.
explanation:
Smallpox had afflicted humanity for at least 3,000 years and, by WHO's estimate, killed some 300 million people in the twentieth century alone. In 1967 the World Health Organization launched an intensified eradication programme, which worked by identifying every case and its contacts and making sure they were vaccinated. Within four years the disease was gone from Latin America; four more years ended it in Asia.

The final naturally acquired case was Ali Maow Maalin, a 23-year-old hospital cook and former vaccinator in Merca, Somalia, who fell ill after guiding a vehicle carrying two infected children in October 1977. He recovered and later worked in Somalia's polio eradication campaign.

After two years of searching for any remaining transmission, an independent Global Commission certified eradication in December 1979, and on 8 May 1980 the World Health Assembly formally declared it. A laboratory accident in Birmingham, England, in 1978 caused the last known cases and one death.

people.name: Health workers, vaccinators and surveillance teams in many countries

whatChanged: Removed a disease from the world entirely, the first time this had been achieved for a human disease.
whyItMattered: Proved that global eradication was possible and shaped later campaigns against polio and Guinea worm.
limitations: Smallpox virus stocks are still held in laboratories, so the risk of release is not zero.
Eradication depended on features specific to smallpox, such as no animal reservoir and visible symptoms, which many diseases lack.

title: First malaria vaccine recommended for children
summary: On 6 October 2021 WHO recommended broad use of the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine for children in areas with moderate to high transmission, based on a pilot programme in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi.
explanation:
From 2019, the health ministries of Ghana, Kenya and Malawi introduced the RTS,S vaccine into routine childhood immunisation in selected areas, as a pilot coordinated by WHO. By the time of the recommendation, the programme had reached more than 800,000 children.

After reviewing two years of data on safety, feasibility and impact, WHO's advisory bodies recommended the vaccine for children in sub-Saharan Africa and other regions with moderate to high transmission of Plasmodium falciparum. It was the first vaccine recommended against any human parasitic disease. A second vaccine, R21/Matrix-M, was recommended in October 2023.

WHO presents the vaccine as an addition to existing tools such as bed nets and prompt treatment, not a replacement for them.

title: Random allocation tests streptomycin for tuberculosis
summary: A Medical Research Council trial published in 1948 assigned patients with pulmonary tuberculosis to streptomycin or to usual care without it using random numbers held in sealed envelopes. It became a model for the randomised controlled trial.
explanation:
When the antibiotic streptomycin became available, the British Medical Research Council organised a trial in several hospitals. The statistician Austin Bradford Hill designed a scheme in which each patient's allocation was decided by random numbers, kept in sealed envelopes marked only with the hospital's name and a number, so that clinicians could not influence who received the drug.

The trial, reported in the British Medical Journal in 1948, found a markedly lower death rate among patients given streptomycin. Its lasting importance lay in its method: concealed random allocation protects comparisons from the conscious and unconscious choices of those running a trial.

Historians note that allocation by alternation had been used in earlier controlled trials, and that the word 'random' sometimes appeared in earlier reports when alternation was actually used.

whyItMattered: The randomised controlled trial became the standard method for evaluating treatments.
limitations: It was not the first controlled trial; alternation had long been used to allocate treatments fairly.
The trial compared streptomycin with usual care only, in a selected group of patients.

title: Insulin first treats a dying boy in Toronto
summary: In 1921–22 a University of Toronto team extracted insulin from the pancreas. On 23 January 1922 a purified extract brought 14-year-old Leonard Thompson's diabetes under control, turning a fatal disease into a treatable one.
explanation:
Type 1 diabetes was then a universally fatal disease. In the summer of 1921 Frederick Banting and Charles Best, working in J. J. R. Macleod's laboratory, showed that a pancreatic extract lowered blood sugar in diabetic dogs. Early presentations did not convince everyone, since earlier investigators had reported similar effects without producing a usable treatment.

On 11 January 1922 Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old near death at Toronto General Hospital, was injected with Banting and Best's extract. It lowered his blood sugar but had little clinical effect. The biochemist James Collip then produced a purer extract, and from 23 January Thompson improved dramatically. He lived another 13 years.

Production was scaled up with the university's Connaught Laboratories and drug companies, and the Nobel Prize of 1923 went to two members of the team, Banting and Macleod, amid lasting disputes over credit.

whyItMattered: One of the first modern instances of a laboratory discovery directly saving lives, and the basis of diabetes treatment ever since.
limitations: Insulin manages diabetes but does not cure it; Thompson died at 27 from complications.

title: Penicillin: from a mould in London to mass production
summary: Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a Penicillium mould killed bacteria. A decade later Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their Oxford team showed it could treat infections, and wartime research in the United States made mass production possible.
explanation:
Returning from holiday in September 1928, Fleming found a culture plate at St Mary's Hospital in London where bacteria had failed to grow around a contaminating mould. He identified it as Penicillium and showed it killed many disease-causing bacteria, but the substance was hard to produce and remained a laboratory curiosity.

From 1939, Florey, Chain, Norman Heatley and others at Oxford developed ways to extract it and showed that it protected infected mice. In 1941 an Oxford police constable became the first person treated; he improved but died when supplies ran out.

With Britain at war, production research moved to the United States, including the Department of Agriculture laboratory in Peoria, Illinois, and drug companies that developed deep-tank fermentation. Penicillin was produced at scale from 1944. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.

title: Oral rehydration: sugar and salt water against cholera
summary: Trials in Dhaka in 1968 showed that a solution of glucose and salt taken by mouth could replace much of the intravenous fluid needed in cholera. In 1971, in refugee camps during the Bangladesh Liberation War, Dilip Mahalanabis showed it worked even where families gave it themselves.
explanation:
Untreated cholera killed 30–40 per cent of patients, and intravenous fluids, the only effective treatment, were difficult and costly to provide in large outbreaks. Researchers in Dhaka (then East Pakistan) and Calcutta found that the intestine continues to absorb salt and water in cholera if glucose is present.

At the Cholera Research Laboratory in Dhaka, Richard Cash and David Nalin successfully tested an oral glucose–salt solution in 29 patients, publishing in The Lancet in 1968. In 1971, as refugees fled to India during the war that created Bangladesh, cholera broke out in the camps. Mahalanabis, of the Johns Hopkins centre in Calcutta, used drums of oral solution administered largely by family members, and the case fatality rate fell significantly.

In 1978 The Lancet called the discovery potentially the most important medical advance of the century. Even so, persuading sceptical clinicians that minimally trained people could give it took years.

title: Kangaroo mother care begins in Bogotá
summary: In 1978, faced with overcrowding and too few incubators, neonatologists Edgar Rey Sanabria and Héctor Martínez at Bogotá's Instituto Materno Infantil began keeping small and premature babies in continuous skin-to-skin contact with their mothers.
explanation:
The method has three parts: the baby is held upright against the mother's (or another carer's) bare chest, is breastfed, ideally exclusively, and goes home early with close follow-up. It was devised as an alternative to scarce and sometimes unsafe incubator care.

The idea spread from Colombia to Brazil and well beyond. Randomised trials followed: a Cochrane review of 21 studies including more than 3,000 low-birthweight infants found better growth with kangaroo care, and later reviews report lower mortality compared with standard care, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. WHO now recommends it for clinically stable newborns weighing 2,000 g or less.

Kangaroo care shows a pattern common in medicine: a practical solution from a resource-constrained setting, later confirmed by trials and adopted in wealthy countries too.

limitations: Trial evidence mostly concerns babies who are already clinically stable.
It requires sustained support for mothers and families, which is not always available.

title: Auckland trial shows steroids before birth protect premature babies
summary: In 1972 Graham Liggins and Ross Howie published the first randomised, placebo-controlled trial of giving corticosteroids to mothers at risk of preterm birth. Babies whose mothers received betamethasone had less respiratory distress and lower mortality.
explanation:
The idea came from sheep. Liggins, an obstetrician in Auckland, was infusing pregnant ewes with corticosteroids to study what triggers labour. One delivered a lamb so premature it should not have survived, yet it was breathing. Its lungs had matured faster than expected.

With the paediatrician Ross Howie, Liggins designed a double-blind trial at a tertiary obstetric hospital in Auckland: women at risk of preterm birth received betamethasone or a matching placebo. The steroid reduced neonatal respiratory distress syndrome and deaths, and appeared safe in the short term. Follow-up of the trial's children has continued for decades, into adulthood.

Antenatal corticosteroids became a cornerstone of care for threatened preterm birth worldwide, although adoption was slow for years after the trial, and questions about timing and dose are still being studied.

people.name: Women and babies in the Auckland Steroid Trial

whatChanged: Provided randomised evidence that a single course of steroids before birth reduces breathing problems and death in premature babies.
whyItMattered: One of the most effective interventions for preterm birth, now recommended internationally.
limitations: 'First' refers to the first randomised trial of the treatment, as the Liggins Institute describes it; the idea came from Liggins's earlier sheep experiments.
Uptake was slow for many years after publication.
Optimal timing, dose and use in some settings remain under study.

title: The first human heart transplant, Cape Town
summary: In the early hours of 3 December 1967, at Groote Schuur Hospital, a team led by Christiaan Barnard transplanted the heart of Denise Darvall, a 25-year-old killed in a road accident, into Louis Washkansky. He lived for 18 days.
explanation:
Barnard had established an open-heart surgery programme at Groote Schuur Hospital and the University of Cape Town in 1958. Several teams in the United States had prepared for heart transplantation through years of animal research and were close to attempting it.

Denise Darvall was struck by a car outside a bakery in Observatory, Cape Town, and declared brain dead. Her heart was transplanted into Louis Washkansky, a 54-year-old with severe heart failure, and was shocked into beating just before 6 a.m. on 3 December. He died 18 days later of pneumonia. Barnard's second patient, Philip Blaiberg, lived for about 19 months.

The operation drew worldwide attention, and surgeons elsewhere, including Euryclides Zerbini's team in Brazil, began preparing their own transplants within days.

date.basis: Date of the operation at Groote Schuur Hospital, reported in the South African Medical Journal three weeks later.

people.name: Christiaan Barnard and the Groote Schuur heart team
Denise Darvall and her family
people.role: Donor, and the family who consented to donation

whatChanged: Showed that a human heart could be transplanted from one person to another and restart.
whyItMattered: Opened clinical heart transplantation and forced public and professional debate about brain death and organ donation.
limitations: 'First' here means the first transplant of a heart from one person to another. Surgeons in the United States, including Norman Shumway and Adrian Kantrowitz, were also preparing to attempt it.
Early survival was short: Washkansky died of pneumonia, and rejection was not recognised in time.
It built on decades of experimental work by many surgeons, especially in the United States.
harms: The case raised ethical questions, still debated, about how death is defined for organ donation and about experimental surgery on dying patients.

title: Aro village system: psychiatric care in the community
summary: From the mid-1950s, the Nigerian psychiatrist Thomas Adeoye Lambo, at the new Aro hospital in Abeokuta, arranged for patients to live in nearby villages during treatment, working with local communities and traditional healers.
explanation:
The Aro Mental Hospital opened in Abeokuta in 1954, under the British colonial government. Lambo, Nigeria's first Indigenous psychiatrist, had trained in Britain, including at the Maudsley Hospital, and returned in 1952. Rather than confining patients in wards, he arranged for them to live in surrounding villages while attending the hospital for treatment.

The Aro village system built on existing community structures, gave the villages health clinics and infrastructure in return, and drew traditional healers into care. It also supported research, such as the Cornell–Aro project, showing that major psychiatric disorders occurred in Nigeria in ways comparable to elsewhere.

The approach became an influential example of culturally grounded community psychiatry and inspired rehabilitation villages in Tanzania from 1969. Lambo later became Deputy Director-General of the World Health Organization.

whatChanged: Combined hospital psychiatry with village life, family involvement and traditional healing.
whyItMattered: A pioneering model of community mental health care developed in Africa, influential across the continent and internationally.
limitations: This account draws mainly on professional histories; the experiences of patients and host villagers are less well documented.

title: The first CT scan of a patient's brain
summary: On 1 October 1971 at Atkinson Morley's Hospital in London, a prototype scanner built by the EMI engineer Godfrey Hounsfield produced a cross-sectional X-ray image of a living patient's brain, revealing a tumour.
explanation:
Conventional X-rays superimpose everything in their path onto a single picture. Hounsfield, an engineer at EMI, conceived of taking many X-ray measurements from different angles and using a computer to reconstruct a slice through the body. EMI, flush with income from its music business, and the British Department of Health funded the work.

The prototype was installed at Atkinson Morley's Hospital, where the radiologist James Ambrose scanned the first patient on 1 October 1971: the image showed a cystic tumour in the frontal lobe, and the surgeon later confirmed it looked as the picture predicted. Each slice took minutes to acquire and longer to compute, but neurologists around the world quickly sought the new machines.

The physicist Allan Cormack had independently worked out the mathematics of reconstructing images from projections. He and Hounsfield shared the 1979 Nobel Prize.

date.basis: Date of the first clinical scan, as given by the Nobel Foundation and imaging histories.

people.role: Radiologist who performed the first clinical scans

whatChanged: Allowed doctors to see soft tissues such as the brain in cross-section without surgery.
whyItMattered: Transformed diagnosis in neurology and then throughout medicine, and opened the way for later cross-sectional imaging.
limitations: 'First' means the first scan of a patient with Hounsfield's machine. The 1979 Nobel Prize recognised Allan Cormack alongside Hounsfield for developing computer-assisted tomography.
Tomography itself was older; Hounsfield's step was combining X-ray measurement with computer reconstruction.
CT uses ionising radiation, so its benefits must be weighed against radiation dose.

title: Two IVF births in 1978: Oldham and Calcutta
summary: On 25 July 1978 Louise Brown was born in Oldham, England, after in vitro fertilisation by Robert Edwards, Patrick Steptoe and Jean Purdy. Sixty-seven days later, on 3 October, a team in Calcutta led by Subhas Mukhopadhyay announced the birth of Durga (Kanupriya Agarwal).
explanation:
Robert Edwards had pursued the idea of fertilising human eggs outside the body since the 1950s. With the gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe, who retrieved eggs by laparoscopy, and the embryologist and nurse Jean Purdy, he worked through years of experiments and failures. Louise Brown, born at Oldham General Hospital, was the first child conceived through IVF.

In Calcutta, Subhas Mukhopadhyay, with Sunit Mukherjee and the gynaecologist Saroj Kanti Bhattacharya, used a different approach, including ovarian stimulation, and announced the birth of Durga on 3 October 1978. Both announcements met scepticism. The British team went on to further births; Mukhopadhyay was transferred to an eye hospital and could not continue his work. Today his team's work is widely acknowledged as the world's second IVF birth.

IVF has since led to millions of births worldwide. Edwards received the Nobel Prize in 2010.

whyItMattered: Founded assisted reproduction, now used worldwide, and raised enduring ethical and social questions.
limitations: Early IVF involved many failed attempts and years of refinement.

title: Polio vaccines tested on millions of children
summary: In 1954 about 1.8 million children in the United States, Canada and Finland took part in field trials of Jonas Salk's inactivated polio vaccine, announced as safe and effective on 12 April 1955. Albert Sabin's oral vaccine was then tested on a vast scale in the Soviet Union from 1958–59.
explanation:
Polio paralysed 13,000–20,000 people a year in the United States alone in the early 1950s. Salk, at the University of Pittsburgh, made a vaccine from killed poliovirus. The March of Dimes funded a field trial supervised by Thomas Francis Jr. of the University of Michigan: some children received vaccine or an injected placebo, with neither families nor officials knowing which, while others were observed as controls. On 12 April 1955 Francis announced that the vaccine was safe and effective, and it was licensed the same day.

Within weeks, two lots made by Cutter Laboratories turned out to contain live virus. Thousands of people received the faulty vaccine, and some developed paralysis.

Sabin's live, oral vaccine was tested instead, during the Cold War, in the Soviet Union, first on thousands and then on millions of children, before being adopted worldwide.

whyItMattered: Polio vaccination ended wild polio in the Americas by 1994 and underpins the global eradication effort.

The Soviet trials of Sabin's vaccine were large observational field trials rather than placebo-controlled studies.
harms: In the 1955 Cutter incident, faulty vaccine containing live virus was given to thousands of people, and some children were paralysed.

title: Ring vaccination trial against Ebola in Guinea
summary: During the 2013–16 West African Ebola epidemic, the Ebola ça Suffit! trial in Guinea vaccinated contacts, and contacts of contacts, of confirmed cases either immediately or after 21 days. No one vaccinated immediately developed Ebola from ten days onwards.
explanation:
Testing a vaccine during a fast-moving epidemic is difficult. The trial, run by Guinean authorities with WHO, Médecins Sans Frontières and other partners, used ring vaccination, the containment strategy that had helped eradicate smallpox. Each newly confirmed case defined a ring of contacts and contacts of contacts, and rings were randomly assigned to immediate or delayed vaccination with a single dose of rVSV-ZEBOV.

Among those vaccinated immediately there were no cases of Ebola with onset ten or more days after randomisation, while cases did occur in the delayed group. The final results, published in 2017, estimated vaccine efficacy at 100 per cent, with wide statistical uncertainty.

The vaccine was later used in further outbreaks and real-world studies found it highly effective. The trial showed that rigorous evaluation can be done in the middle of an emergency in a low-income country.

date.basis: Trial conducted in 2015; interim results published in 2015 and final results in The Lancet in February 2017.

whyItMattered: Supported the vaccine's use in later Ebola outbreaks and demonstrated a rigorous trial design suited to emergencies.
limitations: The efficacy estimate had wide confidence intervals because the epidemic was waning.
Some researchers questioned aspects of the analysis; later real-world studies supported high effectiveness.
contested: A published letter questioned how efficacy was calculated; subsequent outbreak studies nonetheless found the vaccine highly effective.

title: Alma-Ata declares primary health care the route to 'Health for All'
summary: On 12 September 1978, the International Conference on Primary Health Care in Alma-Ata, in the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic, adopted a declaration calling health a fundamental human right and primary health care the key to health for all.
explanation:
The conference, convened by WHO and UNICEF, brought together delegations from 134 countries. Its declaration defined health broadly, as complete physical, mental and social well-being, and called existing inequalities in health between and within countries politically, socially and economically unacceptable.

It set the goal of 'Health for All by the Year 2000' and argued that this could be reached through primary health care: essential, accessible care close to where people live and work, with community participation and action across sectors beyond health.

The goal was not met, and in the following years many programmes narrowed to selected interventions. But primary health care became a core concept for WHO, and in 2018 the Declaration of Astana, in the same country, reaffirmed Alma-Ata as the foundation for universal health coverage.

date.basis: Date given in the text of the declaration (conference held 6–12 September 1978).

whatChanged: Put primary health care and health equity at the centre of global health policy.
whyItMattered: Shaped four decades of health-system planning and remains the reference point for universal health coverage.
limitations: A declaration is a commitment, not an outcome; 'Health for All by 2000' was not achieved.
Its broad vision was soon narrowed in practice to selected, targeted programmes in many countries.

sources.supports: Adopted on 12 September 1978; health as complete physical, mental and social well-being and a fundamental human right; primary health care as key.

title: The Human Genome Project publishes a draft, then a near-complete sequence
summary: An international consortium of 20 groups in six countries published a draft human genome sequence in 2001 and announced an essentially complete sequence in April 2003, two years ahead of schedule. It covered about 92% of the genome.
explanation:
The Human Genome Project began formally in 1990, when the US National Institutes of Health and Department of Energy published a plan for the first five years of an expected 15-year effort. Sequencing was carried out by the International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium: 20 groups in the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, France, Germany and China. A draft was announced in June 2000 and published in Nature in February 2001, alongside a competing draft from the company Celera Genomics.

In April 2003 the consortium announced an essentially complete sequence, as complete as the sequencing technology of the time allowed. The project also changed scientific practice: the sequence was released publicly shortly after it was produced, under the 1996 Bermuda Principles on open data.

date.basis: Draft announced in June 2000 and published on 15 February 2001; completion announced in April 2003. The project itself began in 1990.

locations.name: Whitehead Institute/MIT Center for Genome Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts

people.name: International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium
people.role: Twenty sequencing groups in six countries

people.name: Francis Collins
people.role: Director of the US National Human Genome Research Institute; de facto leader of the consortium

whatChanged: A reference sequence of the human genome became freely available, so that researchers could locate genes and variants without first mapping and sequencing the region themselves.
whyItMattered: It underpins much of modern genetics, including the search for disease genes and genetic testing, and set a precedent for releasing large biological datasets openly.
limitations: The 2003 sequence was 'essentially complete' but still missed about 8% of the genome, mostly highly repetitive regions; those were finished only in 2022.
The reference was a patchwork from a small number of anonymous donors, so on its own it cannot capture variation between people.

title: The last 8% of a human genome is sequenced
summary: In 2022 the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) Consortium published a complete, gapless 3.055-billion-base-pair sequence of a human genome. It covered every chromosome except Y, including the repetitive regions the Human Genome Project could not finish.
explanation:
The reference human genome released from 2000 onwards covered the gene-rich parts of the chromosomes but left about 8% unfinished: highly repetitive regions such as centromeres and the arrays of ribosomal DNA genes, which the short sequence reads of the time could not piece together. That missing 8% is comparable in size to a whole chromosome.

The T2T Consortium, led by researchers at the US National Human Genome Research Institute, the University of California, Santa Cruz, and the University of Washington, used newer long-read sequencing on a cell line that carries only one copy of each chromosome, which made the repeats easier to assemble. Their main paper, one of six in Science on 1 April 2022, reported gapless sequences for all chromosomes except Y, corrected errors in the earlier reference and added nearly 200 million base pairs of new sequence.

date.basis: Published online in Science on 31 March 2022 (print issue of 1 April 2022).

locations.name: National Human Genome Research Institute, Bethesda

locationNote: The consortium involved many institutions; the map shows the three that led it.

people.name: Adam Phillippy, Karen Miga and Evan Eichler
people.role: Consortium leaders (NHGRI, UC Santa Cruz and University of Washington)

whatChanged: Researchers could study the repetitive parts of the genome, such as centromeres, that had been missing from the reference for two decades, and found more than 2 million additional variants using the new sequence.
whyItMattered: A gap-free reference makes it possible to look for disease-related variation in regions that were previously invisible, and to compare genomes more accurately.
limitations: Chromosome Y was not included in the 2022 paper.
It is the sequence of a single cell line, so on its own it cannot represent variation between people.
"Complete" refers to this one genome; it does not mean that the function of all its sequence is understood.

sources.citation: Nurk S, Koren S, Rhie A, Rautiainen M, et al. The complete sequence of a human genome. Science 376(6588):44–53 (2022).
sources.supports: Complete 3.055-billion-base-pair sequence (T2T-CHM13); gapless assemblies for all chromosomes except Y; remaining 8% of the genome; reference since 2000 covered only the euchromatic fraction; errors corrected; nearly 200 million base pairs of new sequence; ribosomal DNA arrays; NHGRI affiliation of lead authors.

sources.citation: National Institutes of Health. Researchers generate the first complete, gapless sequence of a human genome. News release, 31 March 2022.
sources.supports: Publication date; leadership from NHGRI, UC Santa Cruz and the University of Washington; NHGRI as primary funder; cell line with one copy of each chromosome; longer sequence reads; more than 2 million additional variants; six papers in Science; the last 8% comparable in size to a chromosome.

sources.citation: Green E. The human genome sequence is now complete. NHGRI Director's Page, 7 April 2022.
sources.supports: Human Genome Project sequence of 2003 accounted for about 92% of the genome; T2T papers published on 1 April 2022.
